Model the flow as steady, one-dimensional, isentropic air treated as a calorically perfect ideal gas.
Use specific heat ratio gamma equals 1.4 and gas constant R equals 287 J per kg per K.
Inlet Mach number M1 equals 2.0 on the supersonic branch.
Geometry is a converging nozzle with area ratio A2 over A1 equal to 0.7.
Recognize that a converging area decelerates a supersonic stream, so the exit Mach M2 lies on the supersonic branch with M2 less than M1 and greater than 1 (flow moves toward Mach 1, not away).
Apply the isentropic area-Mach relation A over A star equals (1 over M) times the bracket (2 plus (gamma minus 1) M squared) over (gamma plus 1), raised to the exponent (gamma plus 1) over (2 (gamma minus 1)).
Compute A1 over A star from M1 equals 2.0; the value is 1.6875.
Compute A2 over A star as 0.7 times A1 over A star; the value is 1.18125.
Solve the area-Mach equation on the supersonic branch to find the unique M2 whose area ratio equals 1.18125; the expected solution is M2 approximately 1.507.
Use constant stagnation temperature T0 with the isentropic temperature relation T over T0 equals 1 over (1 plus 0.2 M squared) to determine the static temperature ratio T2 over T1 equals 1.8 over (1 plus 0.2 M2 squared).
Compute the velocity ratio V2 over V1 equals (M2 over M1) times the square root of (T2 over T1); the expected value is about 0.8384.
Report the numeric exit Mach number M2.
Report the velocity change Delta V equals V2 minus V1 as a negative quantity, presented either as the ratio V2 over V1 or as a percentage decrease of V1 (approximately a 16.2 percent reduction).
Explicitly state that the velocity change is a decrease (Delta V is negative) and that the supersonic flow is decelerated by the converging area, correcting the original problem framing that asked for an increase.
Do not invent a numerical value for stagnation temperature T0; present the exit velocity only in relative form (velocity ratio or percentage change of V1) unless a numeric T0 or T1 is supplied.
